artpig-01-c1.text: National Gallery. Medium (glossary). National Gallery, London.
artpig-01-c1.quote: Paint is made by mixing a pigment, which is the source of colour, with a medium, which binds the particles of pigment together.
artpig-01-c1.claim: As the National Gallery in London explains, paint is made by mixing a pigment, which supplies the colour, with a medium, which binds the particles of pigment together.

artpig-01-c1.text: Megan M.F. Everhart (2022). Poison books: arsenic in bindings, covers, pigments and dyes. UDaily, University of Delaware.
artpig-01-c1.quote: Both change an object’s color, but simply speaking, dyes are soluble and usually absorbed by the material, while pigments are insoluble and lie on top of the material.
artpig-01-c1.claim: Conservators at the University of Delaware put it this way: dyes are soluble and usually absorbed by the material, while pigments are insoluble and lie on top of it.

artpig-01-c2.text: University of the Witwatersrand (2011). 100,000-year-old ochre toolkit and workshop discovered in South Africa. ScienceDaily.
artpig-01-c2.quote: An ochre-rich mixture, possibly used for decoration, painting and skin protection 100,000 years ago, and stored in two abalone shells, was discovered at Blombos Cave in Cape Town, South Africa.
artpig-01-c2.claim: In 2008 a team led by Christopher Henshilwood uncovered a workshop there where people had made an ochre-rich paint about 100,000 years ago and stored it in two abalone shells.

artpig-01-c2.text: Iker Marcaida, Maite Maguregui, Héctor Morillas, Silvia Perez-Diez, Juan Manuel Madariaga (2019). Raman imaging to quantify the thermal transformation degree of Pompeian yellow ochre caused by the 79 AD Mount Vesuvius eruption. Analytical and Bioanalytical Chemistry.
artpig-01-c2.quote: Most of the wall paintings from Pompeii are decorated with red and yellow colors but the thermal impact of 79 AD Mount Vesuvius eruption promoted the partial transformation of some yellow-painted areas into red.
artpig-01-c2.claim: Most of the wall paintings from Pompeii are decorated with red and yellow colours, but the eruption of Vesuvius in 79 AD changed some of them.

artpig-01-c3.text: National Gallery. Tempera (glossary). National Gallery, London.
artpig-01-c3.quote: It was often combined with oil painting in late 15th-century Italy, but became less common after 1500.
artpig-01-c3.claim: According to the National Gallery it has been used since Antiquity, most early Italian paintings are in it, and it became less common after 1500.

artpig-01-c3.text: Physics World (2008). Synchrotron proves Europeans were not the first painters to use oils. Physics World.
artpig-01-c3.quote: But it has long been recognised that oil painting was documented in the 12th century or even earlier and may have originated outside Europe.
artpig-01-c3.claim: Oil painting was documented by the 12th century, and in 2008 scientists at the European Synchrotron Radiation Facility in Grenoble found drying oils in Buddhist murals from the caves of Bamiyan in Afghanistan, behind the giant Buddha statues the Taliban destroyed in 2001.

artpig-01-c3.text: European Synchrotron Radiation Facility (2008). Synchrotron light unveils oil in ancient Buddhist paintings from Bamiyan. ESRF.
artpig-01-c3.quote: The scientists discovered that 12 out of the 50 caves were painted with oil painting technique, using perhaps walnut and poppy seed drying oils.
artpig-01-c3.claim: Twelve of the 50 caves were painted in oil, perhaps walnut and poppy-seed oil, which the team called the earliest clear example of oil painting in the world.

artpig-02-c1.text: Washington State University (2025). Researchers recreate ancient Egyptian blues. WSU Insider, Washington State University.
artpig-02-c1.quote: A team of Washington State University-led researchers has recreated the world’s oldest synthetic pigment, called Egyptian blue, which was used in ancient Egypt about 5,000 years ago.
artpig-02-c1.claim: Egyptian blue is a calcium copper silicate, CaCuSi₄O₁₀, and it is the oldest synthetic pigment known, already in use in Egypt around 3000 BCE.

artpig-02-c1.text: Washington State University (2025). Researchers recreate ancient Egyptian blues. WSU Insider, Washington State University.
artpig-02-c1.quote: The researchers found that, in fact, to get the bluest color requires only about 50% of the blue-colored components.
artpig-02-c1.claim: The researchers found that the bluest colour requires only about 50 per cent of the blue compound itself; the rest of each grain can be other material.

artpig-02-c2.text: Archaeology Magazine (2024). The Parthenon's Paint Job. Archaeology (Archaeological Institute of America).
artpig-02-c2.quote: This involved exposing them to red or green light, which causes even the smallest particles of the pigment to emit infrared radiation that can be detected using a digital camera.
artpig-02-c2.claim: Shine red or green light on it and it emits infrared radiation, invisible to your eyes but easy for a digital camera to record.

artpig-02-c2.text: King's College London (2023). Scientific analysis reveals the true colours of the Parthenon Sculptures. King's College London News.
artpig-02-c2.quote: This meant for a long time many believed that ancient Greek art only used white marble.
artpig-02-c2.claim: For a long time many people believed that ancient Greek art used only white marble, partly because paint wears away outdoors and partly because restorers sometimes removed surviving traces to restore an assumed original whiteness.

artpig-02-c3.text: Vitruvius (trans. Joseph Gwilt). On Architecture, Book VII. LacusCurtius (University of Chicago).
artpig-02-c3.quote: Thus the copper and sand heating together by the intensity of the fire, impart to each other their different qualities, and thereby acquire their blue colour.
artpig-02-c3.claim: Thus the copper and sand heating together by the intensity of the fire, impart to each other their different qualities, and thereby acquire their blue colour.

artpig-02-c3.text: Washington State University (2025). Researchers recreate ancient Egyptian blues. WSU Insider, Washington State University.
artpig-02-c3.quote: After the Egyptians, the pigment was used by Romans, but by the Renaissance period, the knowledge of how it was made was largely forgotten.
artpig-02-c3.claim: Analysts have found it in a few medieval and even Renaissance paintings, but by the Renaissance the knowledge of how it was made was largely forgotten.

artpig-03-c1.text: University of York (2019). Ultramarine pigment may reveal forgotten female scribes of medieval monasteries. University of York News.
artpig-03-c1.quote: Ultramarine pigment is made from the precious stone lapis lazuli, which was only mined in Afghanistan in the medieval period.
artpig-03-c1.claim: In the Middle Ages it was mined only in Afghanistan, in the mines of Badakhshan, and pigment from there travelled more than 6,000 km to reach Germany.

artpig-03-c1.quote: The intense and unique blue color is caused by the unpaired electron in the sulfur radical anions S3-.
artpig-03-c1.claim: So the colour comes not from a metal ion, as in Egyptian blue, but from a radical, a species with an odd electron.

artpig-03-c2.text: National Gallery. Michelangelo, 'The Entombment (or Christ being carried to his Tomb)'. National Gallery, London.
artpig-03-c2.quote: Michelangelo would have needed ultramarine blue made from the semi-precious stone lapis lazuli to complete the missing figure of the Virgin, as her mantle is traditionally painted this colour.
artpig-03-c2.claim: The gallery's explanation is that Michelangelo would have needed ultramarine made from lapis lazuli for her mantle, and may have been waiting until the last moment to add it, because it was the most expensive pigment and possibly hard to obtain.

artpig-03-c2.text: Associated Press (2020). Hi-tech scans uncover new details of 'Girl with a Pearl Earring,' but not her identity. PBS NewsHour.
artpig-03-c2.quote: They even confirmed once and for all that the girl has eyelashes and revealed that she is painted in front of a green curtain that has faded from view.
artpig-03-c2.claim: In fact Vermeer painted her in front of a green curtain, which has faded from view over the centuries.

artpig-03-c3.text: University of York (2019). Ultramarine pigment may reveal forgotten female scribes of medieval monasteries. University of York News.
artpig-03-c3.quote: Inspection of the women’s teeth revealed more than 100 particles of deep blue colour, encased within fragments of her dental calculus.
artpig-03-c3.claim: Trapped in her hardened plaque, the dental calculus, were more than 100 particles of a deep blue.

artpig-03-c3.text: University of York (2019). Ultramarine pigment may reveal forgotten female scribes of medieval monasteries. University of York News.
artpig-03-c3.quote: the pigments may have gotten into the woman’s mouth as she repeatedly licked her brush into a fine point in order to paint intricate detail on manuscripts
artpig-03-c3.claim: The researchers suggest the pigment entered her mouth as she repeatedly licked her brush to a fine point to paint intricate detail on manuscripts, a technique mentioned in artists' manuals of the time.

artpig-04-c1.text: Joel L. Wolk, Aryeh A. Frimer (2010). Preparation of Tyrian Purple (6,6′-Dibromoindigo): Past and Present. Molecules.
artpig-04-c1.quote: Paul Friedländer, who in 1909 first identified the structure of the dye as 6,6′-dibromoindigo, required 12,000 Murex brandaris snails to produce 1.4 g of pure pigment
artpig-04-c1.claim: When the chemist Paul Friedländer first identified its structure in 1909, he needed 12,000 snails of the species Murex brandaris to produce 1.4 grams of pure dye.

artpig-04-c1.text: Associated Press (2020). Hi-tech scans uncover new details of 'Girl with a Pearl Earring,' but not her identity. PBS NewsHour.
artpig-04-c1.quote: the red is cochineal, made from bugs that live on cactus plants in Mexico and South America
artpig-04-c1.claim: Vermeer's red in Girl with a Pearl Earring is cochineal, made from bugs that live on cactus plants in Mexico and South America.

artpig-04-c2.text: Charlotte Martin de Fonjaudran, Angela Acocella, Gianluca Accorsi, Diego Tamburini, Giovanni Verri, Amarilli Rava, Samuel Whittaker, Francesco Zerbetto, David Saunders (2017). Optical and theoretical investigation of Indian yellow (euxanthic acid and euxanthone). Dyes and Pigments.
artpig-04-c2.quote: states that the pigment derives from the urine of cows fed solely on mango leaves
artpig-04-c2.claim: One of the most frequently cited accounts, published by T. N. Mukharji in 1883, says the pigment came from the urine of cows fed solely on mango leaves.

artpig-04-c2.text: Charlotte Martin de Fonjaudran, Angela Acocella, Gianluca Accorsi, Diego Tamburini, Giovanni Verri, Amarilli Rava, Samuel Whittaker, Francesco Zerbetto, David Saunders (2017). Optical and theoretical investigation of Indian yellow (euxanthic acid and euxanthone). Dyes and Pigments.
artpig-04-c2.quote: glucuronic acid metabolised by mammals such as cows or rabbits and be excreted as a salt of EA
artpig-04-c2.claim: Early studies showed that mammals such as cows or rabbits can combine it with glucuronic acid, one of the body's standard ways of tagging a molecule for disposal, and excrete the product as a salt of euxanthic acid.

artpig-04-c3.text: National Geographic (2016). Was This Masterpiece Painted With Ground Mummy?. National Geographic.
artpig-04-c3.quote: From at least the 16th century until as late as the early 1900s, a pigment made from mummified human remains appeared on the palettes of European artists, including Delacroix.
artpig-04-c3.claim: From at least the 16th century until the early 1900s, European painters could buy a rich, transparent brown called mummy brown, made from ground-up Egyptian mummies, typically mixed with a drying oil such as walnut.

artpig-04-c3.text: National Geographic (2016). Was This Masterpiece Painted With Ground Mummy?. National Geographic.
artpig-04-c3.quote: saying that he had discovered it was made of dead Pharaohs and we must bury it accordingly
artpig-04-c3.claim: His nephew Rudyard Kipling remembered him announcing that he had discovered it was made of dead Pharaohs and they must bury it accordingly.

artpig-04-c3.text: National Geographic (2016). Was This Masterpiece Painted With Ground Mummy?. National Geographic.
artpig-04-c3.quote: it’s almost impossible to scientifically determine what specific paintings may feature the pigment, even through the use of mass spectrometry
artpig-04-c3.claim: Delacroix did use mummy brown, but it is almost impossible to show that any specific painting contains it.

artpig-05-c1.text: National Gallery. Lead white (glossary). National Gallery, London.
artpig-05-c1.quote: It was the main white pigment used by artists until the 19th century and was produced artificially by exposing metallic lead to acetic acid in a carbon dioxide-rich environment.
artpig-05-c1.claim: It was the main white pigment used by artists until the 19th century, for grounds, for lightening other colours and for painting light itself.

artpig-05-c1.quote: Strips of metallic lead are placed in porous earthenware pots, over weak acetic acid (vinegar) in sheds with fermenting manure that produce heat and CO2.
artpig-05-c1.claim: Strips of lead were set in porous earthenware pots over weak vinegar, in sheds packed with fermenting manure.

artpig-05-c1.text: Michele Augusto Riva, Alessandra Lafranconi, Marco Italo D’Orso, Giancarlo Cesana (2012). Lead Poisoning: Historical Aspects of a Paradigmatic "Occupational and Environmental Disease". Safety and Health at Work.
artpig-05-c1.quote: Remarkable painters who became victims of lead poisoning may have been Piero della Francesca (c. 1416-1492), Rembrandt (1606-1669), and Francisco Goya (1746-1828)
artpig-05-c1.claim: A 2012 history of lead poisoning by Michele Augusto Riva and colleagues argues that among Renaissance workers the painters were probably the most exposed, and names Piero della Francesca, Rembrandt and Francisco Goya as painters who may have been victims.

artpig-05-c2.text: Marika Spring, Rachel Grout (2002). The Blackening of Vermilion: An Analytical Study of the Process in Paintings. National Gallery Technical Bulletin.
artpig-05-c2.quote: Raman spectroscopy showed that the white material is mercury(I) chloride, calomel, while the black is likely to be metacinnabar, indistinguishable from vermilion itself by Raman techniques.
artpig-05-c2.claim: Raman spectroscopy identified the white as calomel, mercury(I) chloride.

artpig-05-c2.text: Davide Castelvecchi (2013). Paintings Turning Black? Blame Mercury. Scientific American (from Nature).
artpig-05-c2.quote: Now researchers have shown that the culprit is elemental mercury, which forms under exposure to light and chlorine ions in the air.
artpig-05-c2.claim: Salty air and light, in other words, can make liquid metal from red paint.

artpig-05-c3.text: Victoria and Albert Museum. Wallpaper and hygiene: the story of sanitary wallcoverings. V&A.
artpig-05-c3.quote: In 1775, the Swedish chemist Carl Wilhelm Scheele (1742 – 86) discovered a new green pigment that contained arsenic (copper arsenite).
artpig-05-c3.claim: In 1775 the Swedish chemist Carl Wilhelm Scheele discovered a new green pigment that contained arsenic, copper arsenite.

artpig-05-c3.text: National Geographic (2022). These green books are poisonous, and one may be on a shelf near you. National Geographic.
artpig-05-c3.quote: Despite the toxicity of arsenic-based emerald green in household goods, wares, and clothing, it was never prohibited.
artpig-05-c3.claim: Yet emerald green was never actually prohibited.

artpig-05-c3.text: National Geographic (2022). These green books are poisonous, and one may be on a shelf near you. National Geographic.
artpig-05-c3.quote: They found that the bookcloth contained an average of 1.42 milligrams of arsenic per square centimeter.
artpig-05-c3.claim: The bookcloth carried an average of 1.42 milligrams of arsenic per square centimetre; a lethal dose for an adult is roughly 100 milligrams.

artpig-06-c1.text: Alexander Kraft (2018). What a chemistry student should know about the history of Prussian blue. ChemTexts.
artpig-06-c1.quote: It starts with the discovery of this new blue pigment by the color maker and former army officer Johann Jacob von Diesbach and the theologian and alchemist Johann Conrad Dippel in 1706 in Berlin.
artpig-06-c1.claim: In Berlin in 1706 a colour maker and former army officer, Johann Jacob Diesbach, and the theologian and alchemist Johann Conrad Dippel came upon a new blue.

artpig-06-c1.quote: It is the oldest modern synthetic pigment that has been in use since its discovery in 1704 until the present day.
artpig-06-c1.claim: Named after its home, Prussian blue (or Berlin blue) is the oldest modern synthetic pigment, and it is still in use today.

artpig-06-c1.text: Ilana Singer Blaine (2017). The Blue Era. Tikotin Museum of Japanese Art.
artpig-06-c1.quote: In fact, it was brought to Edo only in 1829 and there too was first used in surimono prints.
artpig-06-c1.claim: Dutch traders carried it to Japan, where it was called Berurin-ai, Berlin blue, and it reached Edo (now Tokyo) in 1829.

artpig-06-c1.text: Ilana Singer Blaine (2017). The Blue Era. Tikotin Museum of Japanese Art.
artpig-06-c1.quote: Indeed, ten prints from the series, "Thirty-Six Views of Mount Fuji," among them, the print known as "The Great Wave at Kanagawa," were printed in Prussian blue.
artpig-06-c1.claim: In 1831 the publisher Nishimuraya Yohachi advertised Katsushika Hokusai's new series Thirty-Six Views of Mount Fuji as prints "in blue", and ten prints from the series, including the Great Wave, were printed in Prussian blue.

artpig-06-c2.quote: The French chemist Louis Vauquelin discovered the element chrome in 1797.
artpig-06-c2.claim: In 1797 the French chemist Louis Vauquelin discovered the element chromium.

artpig-06-c2.quote: Even though Jean Baptiste Guimet’s process for producing artificial ultramarine blue costs 400 francs per kilo, he is awarded the Société prize.
artpig-06-c2.claim: In February 1828 the prize went to Jean-Baptiste Guimet, even though his process cost 400 francs a kilo, while genuine ultramarine was fetching up to 4,000.

artpig-06-c3.text: Mathew Lyons (2023). John Goffe Rand Invents Paint Tubes. History Today.
artpig-06-c3.quote: On 11 September 1841, John Goffe Rand patented the ‘metal rolls for paint’, sparking a revolution in oil painting.
artpig-06-c3.claim: On 11 September 1841 he patented "metal rolls for paint": collapsible tubes of thin metal, best made of tin, with a screw cap.

artpig-06-c3.text: William B. Ashworth, Jr. Scientist of the Day: John Goffe Rand. Linda Hall Library.
artpig-06-c3.quote: In fact, artists had been painting en plein air for several decades, especially in France, and I suspect that portable easels and paint boxes were just as important as the paint tube in allowing painters access to the countryside.
artpig-06-c3.claim: Artists had been painting in the open air for several decades before, especially in France, and portable easels and paint boxes may have mattered just as much.

artpig-07-c1.text: Van Gogh Museum. Vincent van Gogh, The Bedroom. Van Gogh Museum, Amsterdam.
artpig-07-c1.quote: The walls and doors, for instance, were originally purple rather than blue.
artpig-07-c1.claim: Today you see blue walls and doors, but according to the Van Gogh Museum the walls and doors were originally purple rather than blue, and much of the strong contrast you see now is the result of discolouration.

artpig-07-c1.text: ColourLex. Vincent van Gogh, Bedroom in Arles. ColourLex.
artpig-07-c1.quote: Both the walls and doors were initially of a distinct violet colour and were painted in cobalt blue with mixed in carmine (cochineal) lake.
artpig-07-c1.claim: Analysis published by Johanna Salvant showed that the walls and doors were painted in cobalt blue mixed with carmine, a cochineal red lake.

artpig-07-c1.text: Federica Pozzi, Elena Basso, Silvia A. Centeno, Louisa M. Smieska, Nobuko Shibayama, Roy Berns, Megan Fontanella, Lena Stringari (2021). Altered identity: fleeting colors and obscured surfaces in Van Gogh's Landscapes in Paris, Arles, and Saint-Rémy. Heritage Science.
artpig-07-c1.quote: Among these red lake pigments, eosin red, commercially known as geranium lake and one of the most prone to fading, has been the focus of relatively recent studies
artpig-07-c1.claim: Eosin, sold as geranium lake, was reportedly one of his favourite pigments, and it is one of the red lakes most prone to fading.

artpig-07-c2.text: L. Monico, K. Janssens, E. Hendriks, F. Vanmeert, G. Van der Snickt, M. Cotte, G. Falkenberg, B. G. Brunetti, C. Miliani (2015). Van Gogh's Sunflowers: evidence of degradation of the chrome yellows. ESRF Highlights 2015.
artpig-07-c2.quote: The darkening of the yellow colours in Van Gogh’s Sunflowers (Van Gogh Museum, Amsterdam) has been strongly debated over the past few decades.
artpig-07-c2.claim: For decades experts debated whether the differences in yellow between versions were Van Gogh's choice or damage.

artpig-07-c2.text: L. Monico, K. Janssens, E. Hendriks, F. Vanmeert, G. Van der Snickt, M. Cotte, G. Falkenberg, B. G. Brunetti, C. Miliani (2015). Van Gogh's Sunflowers: evidence of degradation of the chrome yellows. ESRF Highlights 2015.
artpig-07-c2.quote: about 35% of CrIII-species are present as a 2-3 µm thick layer right at the varnish/paint interface, while only CrVI-compounds constitute the yellow paint underneath
artpig-07-c2.claim: In one region, about 35 per cent of the chromium was Cr(III) in a layer 2–3 micrometres thick, right where the paint meets the varnish, while the yellow paint beneath was unchanged.

artpig-07-c3.text: NPR (2016). A Chemist Accidentally Creates A New Blue. Then What?. WNYC / NPR.
artpig-07-c3.quote: In 2009, as part of his lab at Oregon State University, Subramanian — a professor of materials science — was working with students to manufacture new materials that could be used in electronics.
artpig-07-c3.claim: In 2009 Mas Subramanian and his students at Oregon State University were making new materials for electronics, heating mixtures to over 2,000 °F (about 1,100 °C).

artpig-07-c3.text: Hyperallergic (2021). Meet YInMn, the First New Blue Pigment in Two Centuries. Hyperallergic.
artpig-07-c3.quote: An earlier version of this article identified YInMn as the first shade of blue created in 200 years.
artpig-07-c3.claim: Hyperallergic, which once described it that way, corrected itself: it is the first new inorganic blue pigment in that time, the last having been cobalt blue in the early 19th century.

artpig-07-c3.text: Dezeen (2016). Anish Kapoor flaunts use of "world's pinkest pink" despite personal ban from its creator. Dezeen.
artpig-07-c3.quote: Kapoor’s Vantablack is currently the blackest substance known – so dark that it absorbs 99.96 per cent of light.
artpig-07-c3.claim: It is made of microscopic vertical tubes: light that strikes it is trapped between them instead of bouncing back, and it absorbs about 99.96 per cent of the light.

artpig-07-c3.text: MIT News (2019). MIT engineers develop "blackest black" material to date. MIT News.
artpig-07-c3.quote: The foil captures at least 99.995 percent* of any incoming light, making it the blackest material on record.
artpig-07-c3.claim: Then, in 2019, MIT engineers grew a carbon nanotube coating that captures at least 99.995 per cent of incoming light, ten times blacker, and used it to make a $2 million yellow diamond look like a flat black void.
